title: Satin shading
subtitle: Blending colours across a filled shape using rows of flat satin
excerpt: Satin shading builds colour gradients by laying rows of flat satin stitch in different shades, each row interlocking with the last so the joins disappear into the blend.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), shaded embroidery chapter (Project Gutenberg #20776).

glossaryTerms.definition: Rows of satin stitch where the stitches of each new row are placed between the stitches of the previous row, hiding the boundary line.
A sequence of thread colours ordered from lightest to darkest (or darkest to lightest) used to build a gradient across a filled shape.

heroPrompt: Satin shading on a petal shape, three shades of pink blending from deep rose at the base to pale blush at the tip, close view, natural light.

content.text: Satin shading works by placing each new row of stitches so they form
with the previous row. Lay the first row along the outer edge of the shape, then work each successive row with stitches that fall between those already placed. Pick a
of 3 to 5 values from dark to light before you start. The colours blend because the transition line is broken up rather than cut clean.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton in 3 to 5 shades of one colour, 2 strands

content.text: Outline the petal shape lightly with a water-soluble pen. Divide the shape into three rough bands: base, middle, and tip.
Thread with your deepest shade. Work the first row of flat satin stitches across the base band, all stitches angled at roughly 45 degrees and lying parallel.
Switch to your mid shade. Work the next row so each stitch lands between two stitches of the first row, overlapping slightly into the edge of the first row.
Continue into the tip with your lightest shade, again interlocking with the row below.
Finish off each thread at the back with a small weave through the existing stitches. Do not knot.

items.symptom: A hard line appears between colour rows
items.cause: New stitches are placed beside the existing ones rather than between them.
items.fix: Push the needle tip between the existing stitches on the row above. The interlock hides the transition.

items.cause: Stitches are too long and the thread has piled up.
items.fix: Keep individual stitches under 8 mm. Split longer shapes into smaller zones.

content.text: Satin shading is the technique behind realistic petal and leaf fills in needlepainting. The same interlocking principle applies in long-and-short stitch, which extends the rows further into a large shape.
